title: WHAT IF THE CHRISTIANITY YOU INHERITED IS NOT THE CHRISTIANITY JESUS ACTUALLY TAUGHT?
paragraphs: WHAT IF THE CHRISTIANITY YOU INHERITED IS NOT THE CHRISTIANITY JESUS ACTUALLY TAUGHT?

You can inherit a Bible, memorize the right prayers, attend church your entire life, and still miss the heart of the Savior you claim to follow. The most frightening deception may not be the faith you rejected—but the faith you never thought to question.
There is a question that can shake a person's entire spiritual foundation.
Not because it attacks Christianity.
But because it forces us to ask whether we have truly understood Christ.
What if some of the things you were taught to call Christianity were never actually taught by Jesus?
What if the faith you inherited was a mixture of biblical truth, family tradition, cultural expectations, human opinions, and religious habits that nobody ever encouraged you to examine?
What if you have spent years defending things Jesus never commanded while quietly neglecting the very things He said mattered most?
And what if, after all those years of attending church, singing worship songs, quoting Scripture, and trying to be a good Christian, you finally opened the Gospels with fresh eyes...
And discovered a Jesus who was far more holy, far more compassionate, far more confronting, and far more beautiful than the version you had been given?
That discovery could break your heart.
It could also save you from spending the rest of your life confusing religious familiarity with genuine discipleship.
Because there is something more dangerous than not knowing what Jesus taught.
It is being so certain that you already know Him that you stop listening to Him.
And before you dismiss this as another criticism of the Church, understand something important.
This is not an invitation to abandon Christianity.
It is an invitation to return to Christ.
Not to a fashionable reinterpretation of Jesus.
Not to a version of Him that approves of everything we want.
Not to a faith without holiness, repentance, obedience, or truth.
But to the Jesus who actually walked the roads of Galilee, touched the untouchable, confronted religious hypocrisy, called sinners to repentance, died for our sins, and rose again.
The Jesus revealed in Scripture.
The Jesus who is still calling people to follow Him.
And perhaps the most uncomfortable part of that invitation is this:
He may be asking you to surrender some things you have always called sacred.
Not because they are necessarily evil.
But because they have quietly taken the place that belongs to Him alone.
Imagine a child growing up in a Christian home.
Every Sunday, the family attends church.
The child learns when to stand, when to sit, when to bow, and when to say amen.
They learn which clothes are appropriate, which people are considered respectable, which questions are discouraged, and which behaviors make someone look like a good Christian.
They learn Bible verses.
They learn worship songs.
They learn the language of faith.
But somewhere along the way, they also learn something nobody intended to teach them.
They learn that looking holy can sometimes matter more than being honest.
They learn to hide their struggles because struggling might disappoint the people who admire their faith.
They learn that doubt is dangerous, confession is embarrassing, and asking difficult questions can make others uncomfortable.
So they become skilled at appearing spiritually healthy.
They know how to smile in church while falling apart at home.
They know how to say, "God is good," while secretly wondering whether God still wants anything to do with them.
They know how to encourage everyone else while carrying a shame they have never dared to confess.
And eventually, they begin to wonder:
Is this really what following Jesus is supposed to feel like?
Maybe you know that person.
Maybe you raised that person.
Maybe you married that person.
Maybe you are that person.
And if you are, please keep reading.
Because the Jesus of the Gospels has something to say to people who are exhausted from carrying a religion that has become heavier than the hope it was supposed to proclaim.
In Matthew 11:28, Jesus says:
"Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest." (KJV)
Notice what He does not say.
He does not say, "Come to Me once you have convinced everybody you are spiritually successful."
He does not say, "Come to Me when your reputation is repaired."
He does not say, "Come to Me after you have learned how to hide your weaknesses."
He says, "Come unto me."
The invitation is personal.
The Savior is the destination.
And the rest He promises is not permission to remain enslaved to sin. It is the beginning of learning from the One whose yoke is easy and whose burden is light.
Jesus continues by calling us to take His yoke and learn from Him.
He does not remove discipleship.
He rescues us from trying to carry it without Him.
That distinction changes everything.
Because Christianity was never meant to be a performance in which exhausted sinners compete to look the most redeemed.
It is the life of people who have been rescued by grace and are learning to follow their Redeemer.
And that brings us to a confrontation Jesus Himself made.
In Mark 7, religious leaders questioned why His disciples did not follow certain traditional washing practices.
Jesus did not condemn every tradition.
He confronted something much more serious.
Human traditions had been elevated in ways that displaced God's commandments.
In Mark 7:8, He declares:
"For laying aside the commandment of God, ye hold the tradition of men." (KJV)
Let those words settle.
It is possible to be fiercely loyal to a religious tradition while becoming disobedient to the God that tradition claims to honor.
The Greek text uses the word paradosis (παράδοσις), meaning something handed down or transmitted.
A tradition.
An inheritance.
Something received from those who came before us.
Tradition itself is not automatically sinful. The New Testament also speaks positively about faithful apostolic teaching handed down to believers, as in 2 Thessalonians 2:15.
The problem is not that something was inherited.
The problem is what happens when what was inherited contradicts, obscures, or replaces what God has revealed.
That is why the question is not simply, "What did my parents believe?"
Or, "What has my denomination always practiced?"
Or even, "What does my pastor say?"
The deeper question is:
What does Scripture actually teach, and am I willing to obey it even when it challenges what I have always assumed?
This is not rebellion against godly authority.
It is submission to the highest authority.
And the Bereans in Acts 17:11 give us a beautiful example. They received the apostolic message eagerly while examining the Scriptures to see whether what they heard was true.
They were neither blindly gullible nor proudly dismissive.
They listened.
They examined.
They sought the truth.
Imagine what would happen if more Christians approached their faith that way.
Not with arrogance.
Not with a hunger to expose everyone else's errors.
But with an open Bible and a humble prayer:
"Lord, if I have misunderstood You, teach me. If I have defended something You never commanded, correct me. If I have ignored something You clearly said, give me the courage to obey."
That prayer may be more costly than we realize.
Because sometimes the greatest obstacle to spiritual growth is not ignorance.
It is the fear of discovering that we have been wrong.
And Jesus was never afraid to confront that fear.
Consider the people who made Him angry.
Not every religious leader was corrupt. Some sought Him sincerely, and others eventually believed.
But the Gospels repeatedly show Jesus confronting leaders who used religious authority without reflecting God's heart.
In Matthew 23:23, He rebukes those who meticulously tithed small herbs while neglecting the weightier matters of the law: judgment, mercy, and faith.
He does not dismiss obedience.
He exposes selective obedience.
The kind that becomes meticulous about visible details while remaining careless about the condition of the heart.
The kind that can calculate an offering but overlook a wounded neighbor.
The kind that can defend a religious institution while refusing to show mercy to a repentant sinner.
And before we point at the Pharisees, perhaps we should ask whether we have ever done something similar.
Have you ever been more disturbed by someone's clothing than by their suffering?
More concerned about the appearance of your church than the spiritual condition of its people?
More eager to win a theological argument than to speak the truth in love?
More comfortable discussing another person's sin than confessing your own?
These questions are not meant to erase biblical standards.
They are meant to expose how easily we can demand standards from others while avoiding the searching work of God in ourselves.
Jesus never taught that holiness and mercy are enemies.
He embodied both.
He could expose sin without becoming cruel.
He could extend compassion without pretending sin was harmless.
He could welcome the broken without affirming everything that had broken them.
Look at the woman caught in adultery in John 7:53–8:11, a passage whose manuscript history deserves honest acknowledgment because it is absent from some of the earliest surviving Greek manuscripts.

The account has nevertheless been deeply influential in Christian teaching, and its portrayal of mercy alongside a call to leave sin is consistent with themes firmly established elsewhere in the Gospels.
The woman stands exposed.
Accused.
Humiliated.
Surrounded by people who seem more interested in using her situation as a weapon against Jesus than in restoring a human being.
And Jesus refuses to participate in their trap.
He exposes the accusers' own moral vulnerability.
Then He speaks words of mercy and moral seriousness.
"Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more." (John 8:11, KJV)
Do you see it?
No permission to celebrate sin.
No delight in public humiliation.
Mercy.
And a call to transformation.
The Savior does not have to choose between truth and compassion.
He is full of grace and truth.
And perhaps some of us have inherited a Christianity that emphasizes one while treating the other as a threat.
Some have been taught a version of faith so harsh that every mistake feels like the end of their relationship with God.
Others have been taught a version so permissive that repentance is barely mentioned and obedience sounds unnecessary.
Neither distortion does justice to the Gospel.
Grace does not mean sin is insignificant.
The cross reveals how serious sin truly is.
But the cross also reveals how astonishing God's mercy is toward sinners who could never rescue themselves.
Romans 5:8 declares:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us." (KJV)
Not after we became impressive.
Not after our reputation was restored.
Not after we learned every correct religious expression.
While we were yet sinners.
Christ died for us.
And if you have been carrying the secret belief that God only loves the polished version of you, you need to hear that again.
Jesus did not go to the cross because humanity had finally become worthy.
He went because we needed a Savior.
That is not a reason to remain unchanged.
It is the reason real change becomes possible.
The Gospel does not merely offer a new religious identity.
It announces the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ and calls us into a new life through Him.
The apostle Paul writes in Ephesians 2:8–10 that we are saved by grace through faith, not by our works, and that we are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Notice the order.
We do not perform good works to purchase salvation.
We are saved by grace and then called to walk in the good works God has prepared.
Obedience is not the price of being loved by God. It is a fitting response to the grace we have received.
This matters because a Christianity built primarily on fear of human rejection can produce conformity without genuine transformation.
You can change your clothing without surrendering your pride.
You can stop using certain words while continuing to destroy people with your tongue.
You can memorize doctrines while refusing to forgive.
You can donate money while secretly believing your generosity makes you superior.
You can serve in ministry while neglecting the people who live under your own roof.
You can become publicly religious while remaining privately unrepentant.
Jesus knew this.
In Matthew 15:8, He quotes Isaiah:
"This people draweth nigh unto me with their mouth, and honoureth me with their lips; but their heart is far from me." (KJV)
The Hebrew background of this rebuke in Isaiah 29:13 is especially striking.
The word lev (לֵב), commonly translated "heart," carries a rich biblical sense that includes the inner person—thought, intentions, desires, and will.
God is not merely asking whether the right religious words are coming out of our mouths.
He is confronting the inward direction of our lives.
Where is your heart?
What governs your choices when nobody is watching?
What do you love?
What do you excuse?
What do you refuse to surrender?
Who are you becoming?
Because a person can sound devoted to God while remaining deeply resistant to His authority.
And that is where this conversation becomes uncomfortable for all of us.
It is easy to criticize inherited Christianity.
It is much harder to examine the Christianity we are personally practicing.
We can blame our upbringing.
We can blame religious institutions.
We can blame leaders who failed us.
And sometimes those failures were real and serious.
Spiritual abuse, hypocrisy, manipulation, and the misuse of Scripture should never be minimized or excused.
But eventually, we must confront a question that nobody else can answer for us.
Am I actually following Jesus, or am I merely reacting to the people who claimed to represent Him?
Because there is another danger.
Someone wounded by legalism can become so determined never to be controlled again that they begin rejecting every biblical command that feels demanding.
Someone hurt by religious hypocrisy can confuse legitimate criticism of hypocrisy with permission to abandon the Church entirely.
Someone who has suffered under false teaching can become vulnerable to a different false teaching that promises freedom without repentance.
And the enemy of our souls does not care which distortion captures us.
A counterfeit Christianity that crushes people with man-made burdens is dangerous.
A counterfeit Christianity that removes Christ's authority is dangerous too.
Jesus calls us away from both.
Listen to His first recorded proclamation of the kingdom in Mark 1:15:
"The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand: repent ye, and believe the gospel." (KJV)
The Greek word translated "repent" is metanoeite (μετανοεῖτε), from the verb metanoeō.
It carries the idea of changing one's mind or understanding, but biblical repentance is not merely adopting a new opinion.
In the context of Jesus' preaching, it involves a genuine turning toward God that bears fruit in a changed life.
And the word translated "believe" is pisteuete (πιστεύετε), from pisteuō, expressing faith or trust.
Jesus calls people to repent and believe.
Not simply to inherit a religious label.
Not merely to repeat words without understanding.
Not to build a personal spirituality that never challenges their desires.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Trust the King.
Follow Him.
And what is this Gospel?
Paul summarizes its central historical message in 1 Corinthians 15:3–4: Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, was buried, and rose again on the third day according to the Scriptures.
Christianity is not ultimately founded on our emotional experiences, our family customs, or our preferred religious culture.
It is founded on the person and saving work of Jesus Christ.
His life.
His death.
His resurrection.
His lordship.
Everything else must be examined in the light of Him.
This is why Jesus' words in Luke 6:46 are so piercing:
"And why call ye me, Lord, Lord, and do not the things which I say?" (KJV)
There is no comfortable way around that question.
Jesus is not impressed by a title that our lives continually contradict.
Calling Him Lord while deliberately refusing His authority is a contradiction we must take seriously.
But remember the grace of the One asking the question.
He does not confront us because He enjoys destroying sinners.
He confronts us because He calls sinners to life.
He exposes what is false so that we can turn toward what is true.
He brings hidden things into the light so that repentance and healing can begin.
And sometimes the first thing He must dismantle is the religious image we have spent years protecting.
Maybe you have been the person who judges others because you are terrified someone will discover your own failures.
Maybe you have spent years serving in church because you secretly believe God will abandon you if you stop proving your usefulness.
Maybe you have been financially generous but emotionally absent from your family.
Maybe you have defended biblical morality publicly while privately making peace with a sin you refuse to confess.
Maybe you have rejected the Church because people who represented it wounded you, and now even hearing the name of Jesus brings back memories you wish you could forget.
Or maybe you are simply tired.
Tired of pretending.
Tired of knowing the language but feeling far from God.
Tired of carrying questions you have been afraid to ask.
Tired of wondering whether the Christianity you inherited has room for someone as complicated as you.
Listen carefully.
The answer is not to invent a Jesus who never confronts you.
And the answer is not to return to every human expectation that once crushed you.
The answer is to come to the real Christ.
The One who said in John 6:37:
"...him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out." (KJV)
What a promise.
Not that every belief we hold will be affirmed.
Not that every choice we make will be excused.
But that the person who truly comes to Him will not be cast away.
You do not have to arrive with a flawless spiritual résumé.
You come as someone who needs grace.
And you come willing to let the Savior tell you the truth.
There is a beautiful moment in Luke 15 that reveals something of God's heart toward repentant sinners.
A son has squandered his inheritance.
He has dishonored his father.
He has made decisions that leave him desperate, hungry, and humiliated.
Eventually, he comes to himself.
He decides to return home.
He rehearses a confession.
He knows he has sinned.
He has no right to demand restoration on his own terms.
But while he is still a great way off, his father sees him.
And runs.
The father embraces him.
The son confesses.
And the father responds with a celebration of restoration.
The parable does not teach that rebellion was harmless.
It teaches the astonishing joy of restoration when the lost return.
And in the larger context of Luke 15, Jesus tells these parables in response to complaints that He receives sinners and eats with them.
That matters.
Because the religious critics saw scandal.
Jesus revealed the joy of grace.
And this is where our Gospel Warrior theme becomes more than a memorable phrase.
The scandal of a son who dishonored his father.
The grace of a father who welcomed him home.
The scandal of Peter denying the Lord he loved.
The grace of the risen Jesus restoring him and calling him to shepherd His sheep.
The scandal of Saul persecuting believers.
The grace of Christ transforming him into an apostle who proclaimed the Gospel he once opposed.
The scandal of a thief dying beside Jesus, admitting his guilt and turning to the crucified King.
The grace of Jesus promising him paradise.
Not one of these stories tells us that sin does not matter.
They tell us that sin does not have the final word when the Savior intervenes.
And perhaps that is the story you need to hear today.
Because you may have inherited a Christianity that taught you to conceal your scandal at all costs.
Jesus calls you to bring your sin into the light through repentance and faith.
You may have inherited a Christianity that made you believe your failures were the end of your usefulness.
Jesus is able to restore the repentant and shape them into faithful servants.
You may have inherited a Christianity that valued your public image more than your private integrity.
Jesus calls you to truth in the inward person.
And you may have inherited a Christianity that made you fear honest questions.
Jesus invites us to examine His words carefully and respond with faith.
But there is something else we must not miss.
Christianity is not merely about what we leave behind.
It is about whom we follow.
When Jesus called His first disciples, He did not simply hand them a list of religious customs.
He said, "Follow me." (Matthew 4:19, KJV)
That invitation would eventually reshape their priorities, relationships, ambitions, and understanding of the world.
Following Jesus meant learning from Him.
Trusting Him.
Obeying Him.
Being corrected by Him.
And ultimately depending on Him.
It was never meant to be reduced to attending a weekly event while living the rest of our lives as though His words were optional.
Nor was it meant to be reduced to isolated spirituality without fellowship, accountability, worship, or service.
The New Testament calls believers into the body of Christ.
Acts 2:42 describes the early believers continuing in the apostles' teaching, fellowship, breaking of bread, and prayers.
Their faith had doctrine.
It had community.
It had worship.
It had generosity.
It had shared life.
And yes, the early Church had struggles too.
Read the letters to Corinth.
Read Galatians.
Read the warnings in Revelation.
The first Christians were not a flawless community we can romanticize as though they never disagreed or sinned.
But the apostolic writings continually called them back to the same center.
Jesus Christ.
His Gospel.
His truth.
His love.
His holiness.
His lordship.
So perhaps the question is not whether we can recover a perfect religious culture from the past.
Perhaps the question is whether we are willing to be continually corrected by the unchanging truth of God's Word.
Because genuine biblical Christianity is not about finding a community where nobody ever fails.
It is about belonging to Christ and growing with other imperfect believers under the authority of His Word.
And this is why love matters so deeply.
In John 13:35, Jesus says:
"By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another." (KJV)
Not by how impressive our religious vocabulary sounds.
Not by how loudly we condemn the people we dislike.
Not by how successfully we build our own reputation.
By love for one another.
But do not confuse that love with moral indifference.
The same Jesus who commanded love also commanded obedience.
In John 14:15, He says:
"If ye love me, keep my commandments." (KJV)
Love and obedience belong together.
And the love Jesus commands is not merely a feeling.
It is a life shaped by His truth.
A willingness to forgive.
A commitment to serve.
A refusal to exploit.
A concern for the weak.
A desire for holiness.
A readiness to bear one another's burdens.
A faith that becomes visible in how we treat actual human beings.
Including the people who cannot benefit us.
Including those who have disappointed us.
Including those whose wounds make them difficult to love.
That is a Christianity worth recovering.
Not because it is easier.
In many ways, it is far more demanding than maintaining a religious appearance.
It is easier to look righteous for an hour than to love patiently for a lifetime.
It is easier to quote a verse about forgiveness than to forgive someone who has genuinely wounded you.
It is easier to criticize the world than to confront the pride, envy, bitterness, and secret compromise in your own heart.
It is easier to call yourself a disciple than to deny yourself, take up your cross, and follow Jesus.
And yet the life Jesus calls us into is also the life where we discover that His grace is sufficient for our weakness.
We are not saved by becoming impressive disciples.
We are saved by an impressive Savior.
And the grace that saves us also teaches us to renounce ungodliness and live for Him, as Titus 2:11–14 explains.
That is why this message is not about becoming suspicious of every church, pastor, tradition, or Christian family.
There are faithful churches.
There are godly parents.
There are pastors who preach the Word with integrity.
There are traditions that faithfully preserve biblical truth and direct people toward Christ.
Thank God for them.
The goal is not cynicism.
The goal is discernment.
Hold fast to what is good.
Reject what contradicts Scripture.
Remain teachable.
And never mistake your familiarity with Christian culture for the fullness of knowing Christ.
Because one day, the question will not be whether we were impressive defenders of a religious brand.
It will be whether our profession of faith was genuine.
Jesus gives a sobering warning in Matthew 7:21–23 about people who call Him Lord and even appeal to remarkable religious works, yet are exposed as those who practiced lawlessness.
That passage should not be used to torment tenderhearted believers into believing every weakness means they are rejected by God.
But it should awaken anyone who has made peace with hypocrisy while assuming religious activity guarantees salvation.
Christ is not calling us to despair.
He is calling us to examine ourselves honestly and turn to Him.
And if this has exposed something in you, please do not rush past that conviction.
Maybe there is someone you need to forgive.
Maybe there is a sin you need to confess.
Maybe there is a conversation you need to have with your pastor.
Maybe there is a doctrine you need to study more carefully.
Maybe you need to open the Gospel of Mark tonight and read it slowly, asking not merely what you have heard about Jesus, but what the text actually reveals about Him.
Or maybe, for the first time in a long time, you need to stop performing and pray.

"Lord Jesus, I have inherited many things. Some were good. Some may have distorted my understanding of You. Give me discernment to recognize the difference. Forgive my pride, my hypocrisy, my disobedience, and the ways I have used religion to hide from Your truth. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. Teach me to trust You, obey You, love what You love, and follow You faithfully. Restore what has been damaged in my understanding of Your Word. Make me more like You. Amen."
And perhaps this is the moment to be honest with someone else too.
If you have been spiritually exhausted, you do not have to turn your struggle into a polished testimony before you are allowed to ask for prayer.
You do not owe the internet your private history. Share only what you are comfortable sharing.
But perhaps your simple, honest words will remind another struggling believer that they are not the only person learning how to return to the heart of the Gospel.
And please, think of one person who needs this message.
Not someone you want to embarrass.
Not someone you want to win an argument against.
Someone you genuinely love.
A family member who grew up knowing church but no longer knows whether they can trust it.
A friend who has confused religious disappointment with disappointment in Jesus.
A believer who has become weary under impossible expectations.
A young person asking questions nobody seems willing to answer.
Because this conversation should not end when the scrolling stops.
It should lead us back to the Bible.
Back to prayer.
Back to repentance.
Back to fellowship.
Back to Jesus.
That is also why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to replace your local church.
Not to become another voice demanding unquestioning loyalty.
Not to sell a shortcut to spiritual maturity.
But to encourage people to examine Scripture, understand the Gospel, grow in discipleship, and keep Christ at the center of their lives.
And we want those resources to continue reaching people who may never be able to pay for them.
People who are searching for answers.
People rebuilding their faith.
People who cannot afford a shelf full of Christian books.
People who need encouragement to open Scripture again.
This work requires time, resources, and ongoing support.
It is important to be clear about something.
God is glorified through faith in Christ, worship, obedience, love, generosity, and lives transformed by His grace.
Your salvation cannot be purchased, and God's approval is not for sale.
Scripture teaches us to give willingly, not under compulsion. As 2 Corinthians 9:7 says, God loves a cheerful giver.
Not because God needs your money.
But because ministry in this world often depends on people who freely choose to give, serve, and share.
These products can be useful reminders of biblical truth and opportunities to share your faith, but the heart of this ministry will always be the Gospel, not merchandise.
You are still welcome here.
The free resources are still here for you.
Your prayers matter.
Your encouragement matters.
Not as a payment for grace.
Not as proof that you are a better Christian.
But as a willing partnership in making Christ-centered teaching and discipleship resources available to more people.
Because the purpose of Gospel Warrior is not to build an audience that depends on us.
It is to help point people toward the Savior on whom we all depend.
And now, before you leave, return to the question that brought you here.
What if the Christianity you inherited is not entirely the Christianity Jesus actually taught?
Perhaps some of what you inherited was beautiful and true.
Keep it.
Perhaps some of it was merely cultural.
Examine it.
Perhaps some of it was harmful or contrary to Scripture.
Have the courage to reject it.
But do not throw away Jesus because someone misrepresented Him.
Do not confuse the failures of His followers with the failure of His Gospel.
And do not assume that questioning an inherited practice requires questioning the truth of Christ's death and resurrection.
The answer to distorted Christianity is not a Christless spirituality.
It is a deeper, more faithful understanding of Jesus Christ as revealed in Scripture.
The Jesus who welcomes repentant sinners.
The Jesus who confronts hypocrisy.
The Jesus who commands holiness.
The Jesus who shows mercy.
The Jesus who laid down His life for His sheep.
The Jesus who rose from the dead.
The Jesus who remains Lord even when our traditions, institutions, and personal assumptions must be corrected.
And perhaps the greatest tragedy would not be discovering that you misunderstood something about Christianity.
Perhaps it would be discovering that you misunderstood—and then refusing to let Jesus teach you.
So open the Bible again.
Not merely to confirm what you already believe.
Open it ready to be corrected, comforted, convicted, and changed.
Read the words of Christ.
Examine them in context.
Listen to the whole counsel of Scripture.
Seek wise and faithful teachers.
Pray for discernment.
And follow the Savior rather than the applause of any religious crowd.
Because you do not need a more fashionable Jesus.
You do not need a more convenient Jesus.
You do not need a Jesus redesigned to fit your preferences.
You need the real Jesus.
The crucified and risen Lord.
The One who calls sinners to repentance and offers forgiveness through His blood.
The One who can take the wreckage of a life and make something new.

And if you have spent years defending a version of Christianity that left you afraid to approach Him, perhaps today is the day you stop hiding behind what you inherited and begin listening more closely to the One who calls you by His Word.
The most heartbreaking thing would be to spend your life protecting a picture of Jesus while refusing to follow the Jesus who stands before you in Scripture.
